newsitem.title: FRANCE: French to test long "cohabitation" if left wins.
newsitem.headline: French to test long "cohabitation" if left wins.

text.p: French voters will bless five years of power sharing if they elect the left on Sunday to "cohabit" with conservative President Jacques Chirac, but the marriage looks more likely to end in divorce than two predecessors.

"The main unknown issue is whether cohabitation can last five years," constitutional law professor Olivier Duhamel told Reuters. "In the past...those involved avoided triggering a crisis because they could see it would end soon."

The constitutional nuts and bolts of cohabitation got two test runs when late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand shared power with centre-right governments from 1986 to 1988 and from 1993 to 1995.

In past cohabitations, both sides feared that rocking the institutional boat might damage their chances in upcoming presidential elections. The exception was Mitterrand in 1993, who was constrained by having an eye on history.
"Things may be different over five years," Duhamel said.

Former centrist president Valery Giscard d'Estaing warned voters that cohabitation of two antagonistic powers until 2002, when both Chirac's seven-year term and that of the new parliament will run out, would spell disaster for France.
"It will mean the destruction of the institutions of the Fifth Republic," he told France 2 television.
"We would have to say adieu to the political heritage of General (Charles) de Gaulle" who tailored the 1958 constitution giving the president sweeping powers, he said.

Under cohabitation, Chirac would have two heavy punches to offset a lame duck image -- the threat of dissolving parliament again, after a minimum constitutional delay of a year, or resigning and provoking a new presidential election.
Chirac has said he will not resign.

Reversing a previous pledge, Chirac called the National Assembly election 10 months early hoping that voters would re-elect his centre-right allies to give France a "new elan" to help prepare for a single European currency.
But the left scored a stunning upset by winning most votes in a first round of the National Assembly election on May 25 and is well placed to win Sunday's decisive runoff round.

Chirac's first constitutional test would be to choose a prime minister and a cabinet. Duhamel said he is likely to avoid confrontation and appoint Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin as premier as well as the ministers he proposes.

Mitterrand in 1986 appointed Chirac as premier at the start of the first bout of cohabitation but rejected Chirac's nominees for both defence and foreign ministers. Chirac backed down and appointed two technocrats acceptable to Mitterrand.

Jospin will then have to define a government platform and present it to parliament, probably as part of a confidence vote. He has promised to create 700,000 jobs and cut the working week from 39 hours to 35.
Jospin has said his government would be open to all leftist forces of change, ranging from Communists to ecologists, but he is not obliged to include them all.
A minority administration can survive, partly because the 1958 constitution does not demand a government's resignation if it suffers defeat in the day-to-day business of passing laws.

And article 49-3 can give it leverage to push through legislation by tying the government's fate to bills it considers vital. If the article is invoked, the opposition can either give in or call a no-confidence motion which, if passed, topples the government.

The measure was used about a dozen times by former Socialist prime minister Michel Rocard from 1988-91. Rocard, who led a minority excluding Communists, survived several no-confidence motions because the opposition feared a new election.
Jospin has told the Communists, for instance, they must bow to his policies if they want cabinet posts. The Communists oppose a single European currency broadly favoured by Jospin.
